newsitem.title: HONG KONG: PRESS DIGEST-Hong Kong Newspaper Headlines-Jan 7.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-Hong Kong Newspaper Headlines-Jan 7.

text.p: These are some of the leading stories in Hong Kong press on Tuesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

-- ECONOMIC TIMES -- Cheung Kong group launched a reorganisation involving the groups's four listed companies -- Cheung Kong, Hutchison Whampoa, Cheung Kong Infrastructure Holdings and Hongkong Electric Holdings.

-- WEN WEI PO -- Beijing was closely watching developments in the dismantling of the Taiwan provincial government. Authoratative sources said any changes in Taiwan's government structure should be beneficial to the reunification.
-- Chinese Premier Li Peng talked about ten suggestions to help develop poor areas. The poor population in China had been reduced by 200 million from 1987 to 1995.
-- SING TAO -- Former British Foreign Secretary Lord Howe of Aberavon called for reconciliation over the Hong Kong provisional legislature.
-- MING PAO -- From July 1, the Chinese Communist Party's mouthpiece newspaper, the People's Daily, would launch a South China edition to boost its influence in Hong Kong and Macau.

-- With 800,000 people in China receiving their driving licences every year, car rental business was booming. But a lack of regulatory protection meant many cars were stolen and damaged by renters, causing losses to rental centres.
-- EXPRESS NEWS -- Beijing had instructed Shenzhen to carry out a thorough investigation into a case when over 10 deathrow prisoners escapd from a Shenzhen prison during a lunch break.

-- SOUTH CHINA MORNING POST -- Managers of some of the largest public pension funds in the United States, controlling a collective US$250 billion, were coming to Hong Kong this weekend to examine investment opportunites in Hong Kong and China.
-- Shanghai Petrochemical Co, China's largest petrochemical complex, had cashed in on a booming market for Chinese equity to raise $342 million by selling 150 million H shares.
-- HONGKONG STANDARD -- Taxpayers may have to fork out HK$330,000 a month until the handover for each of the 33 provisional legislature members who were also Legislature Councillors.
-- Analysts said China would avoid bold moves in tackling its ailing state enterprises as it focused on stability ahead of this year's crucial Communist Party congress.
